title: The 67-second rule
summary: The CSE is a speed test. Here is the three-pass method that keeps you from losing easy points.
body:
In the Professional exam you have 170 minutes for 170 items, including the descriptive questionnaire. That is about **67 seconds per item**. Subprofessional is even tighter at roughly **58 seconds**.

Most first-time takers fail not because they cannot solve the hard items, but because they spend four minutes on one hard item and never reach ten easy ones.

## The three passes

• **Pass 1:** answer everything you know in under 30 seconds. Do not compute yet if the answer is not obvious.
• **Pass 2:** return to the items that need computation or careful reading.
• **Pass 3:** guess on everything left. There is **no penalty for a wrong answer**, so a blank is always a wasted chance.

## Checkpoints

• After one hour you should be near **item 55**.
• After two hours, near **item 110**.
• If you are behind, stop being careful on items you already know and move.

> **Rule of thumb:** if an item passes **90 seconds**, mark it and move. A hard item should never cost you three easy ones.

## Transfer in blocks

Mark your answers in the booklet first, then transfer in **blocks of ten**. Transferring one item at a time is how people lose their place and shift every answer after it.

title: Grammar traps that cost the most points
summary: Eight agreement and usage rules that show up in almost every CSE verbal section.
body:
Cross out prepositional phrases before you check subject-verb agreement. In _The box of forms is on the table_, the subject is **box**, not **forms**.

## Agreement rules

• **Each, every, either, neither, everyone, somebody, nobody:** singular. _Each of the clerks is present._
• **Either/or and neither/nor:** the verb agrees with the **nearer subject**. _Neither the supervisor nor the clerks were informed._
• **The number of:** singular. **A number of:** plural.
• **One of the** + plural noun takes a singular verb. _One of the applicants is absent._
• **Fewer** for countable things, **less** for mass. _Fewer items, less time._
• **Who** is a subject, **whom** is an object. Test with _he_ or _him_.
• Keep lists **parallel**. _Reading, writing, and speaking_, not _reading, writing, and to speak_.
• An opening phrase must describe the subject right after the comma. _Walking into the office, the clerk noticed the phone_ is correct.

> **The most common trap** is a long phrase between the subject and the verb. Cover the phrase with your finger and read the sentence again.

title: Number series: the 6-step checklist
summary: Work through these six checks in order and most series items fall in under 40 seconds.
body:
Do not stare at the whole sequence. Write the **differences** between consecutive terms above the series.

## The six checks

• **Step 1:** constant difference? That is arithmetic. _4, 8, 12, 16._
• **Step 2:** constant ratio? That is geometric. _3, 6, 12, 24._
• **Step 3:** differences growing by a constant? Check second differences. _2, 6, 12, 20, 30_ is n(n+1).
• **Step 4:** two interleaved series? Look at odd and even positions separately.
• **Step 5:** familiar sets? Squares, cubes, primes, Fibonacci, factorials. _1, 4, 9, 16, 25._
• **Step 6:** digit tricks? Sum of digits, reversed digits, products. _12, 21, 13, 31._

## Useful shortcut

If the jumps are **3, 5, 7, 9**, the next jump is **11**. If the jumps are **2, 4, 8, 16**, the jumps are doubling.

> **Trap:** assuming the first difference pattern holds forever. Always test the pattern on at least two gaps before you commit.

title: Percent word problems without a calculator
summary: Translate English into arithmetic, estimate first, and avoid the two classic traps.
body:
Turn the sentence into an equation.

• **Of** means multiply.
• **Is** means equals.
• **Per** means divide.

## Worked examples

• **20% of 250 is what?** 0.20 x 250 = **50**.
• **45 is what percent of 180?** 45 / 180 = 0.25 = **25%**.
• **Percent change** is change divided by the **original**, never by the new value.
• A **20% discount** means you pay **80%**. One multiplication, not two.
• A **20% increase** followed by a **20% decrease** does not return to the original. It ends at **96%**.

## Estimate first

If the choices are 40, 42, 45, and 48, and your rough answer is a little over 40, pick **42**. You do not need the exact decimal.

> **Useful conversions:** 1/8 = 12.5%, 1/6 is about 16.7%, 1/3 is about 33.3%, 3/8 = 37.5%, 5/8 = 62.5%, 7/8 = 87.5%.

## Two traps

• Answering the **wrong quantity** (asking for males when the question asks for females).
• Dividing by the **new value** in a percent-change item.

title: Conditional logic: the only 3 rules you need
summary: Most logic items are one of three patterns. Learn to name the pattern and the answer is immediate.
body:
Write the conditional as **P → Q**. _If it rains, the trip is cancelled._

## The three patterns

• **Valid:** P → Q, and P is true, so Q is true. _It rained, so the trip is cancelled._
• **Valid:** P → Q, and Q is false, so P is false. _The trip was not cancelled, so it did not rain._ This is the **contrapositive**.
• **Invalid:** P → Q, and Q is true, so P is true. _The trip was cancelled, so it rained._ Other things can cancel a trip.

> **Most common wrong answer:** affirming the consequent. It appears in almost every CSE logic set.

## Syllogisms and assumptions

Draw circles for syllogisms. _All A are B_ puts A inside B. _Some B are C_ puts at least one B in C, but that B might be outside A, so _some A are C_ does not follow.

For assumptions, use the **negation test**. Negate the choice. If the argument collapses, that choice was a necessary assumption.

title: Filing rules that always appear
summary: Alphabetizing looks easy until Dela Cruz and De Leon show up in the same item.
body:
File **letter by letter**, ignoring spaces, hyphens, apostrophes, and punctuation. Compare one character at a time and stop at the first difference.

Dela Cruz becomes **DELACRUZ**. Dela Pena becomes **DELAPENA**. De Leon becomes **DELEON**. Del Rosario becomes **DELROSARIO**.

## Ordering example

Compare the fourth letter: **C, P, E, R**. Alphabetical order is **C, E, P, R**. So the order is Dela Cruz, De Leon, Dela Pena, Del Rosario.

## Rules that decide the order

• **Nothing before something.** _Mabini_ comes before _Mabini, Jr._ because the shorter name has nothing after it.
• Names are filed **last name first**, then first name, then middle initial.
• **Numbers file before letters**, in numerical order. _9_ before _10_ before _100_.
• Treat **Mc** and **Mac** as _Mac_ only if the item's rule says so. Otherwise follow strict letter order.

## Comparing and spelling

Compare from **left to right** and stop at the first mismatch. Watch for **O versus zero**, **I versus lowercase l**, and transposed digits like _6713_ versus _6173_.

> **Spelling drill:** accommodate, definitely, separate, occurred, receive, privilege, maintenance, existence, necessary, embarrass, entrepreneur, liaison, questionnaire, bureaucracy.

title: Constitution articles at a glance
summary: A one-screen map of the 1987 Constitution so article-number questions stop being guesses.
body:
The 1987 Constitution was ratified in a plebiscite on **February 2, 1987**, and has **18 articles**.

## Article map

• **Article I:** National Territory
• **Article II:** Declaration of Principles and State Policies
• **Article III:** Bill of Rights
• **Article IV:** Citizenship
• **Article V:** Suffrage
• **Article VI:** Legislative Department
• **Article VII:** Executive Department
• **Article VIII:** Judicial Department
• **Article IX:** Constitutional Commissions (CSC, COMELEC, COA)
• **Article X:** Local Government
• **Article XI:** Accountability of Public Officers
• **Article XII:** National Economy and Patrimony
• **Article XIII:** Social Justice and Human Rights (includes the CHR)
• **Article XIV:** Education, Science, Technology, Arts, Culture, and Sports

## Key numbers

• The Senate has **24** members serving **six-year** terms, with a maximum of **two** consecutive terms.
• The House has **three-year** terms, with a maximum of **three** consecutive terms.
• The President must be a natural-born citizen, at least **40** years old, a registered voter, able to read and write, and a resident for at least **10 years**.
• The Supreme Court has a Chief Justice and **14** Associate Justices, with mandatory retirement at **70**.

> **Pair the article with its number.** Most items only need the number, not the full text.

title: Exam-day checklist
summary: What to bring, what to leave, and how to spend the last 24 hours.
body:
> Verify every item against your own **Notice of Examination**. CSC adjusts logistics per batch, and your notice is the only version that matters.

## Bring

• Your **Notice of Examination** and a valid government ID.
• **Two black ballpens**, No. 2 pencils, an eraser, and a sharpener.
• A **transparent water bottle**. Avoid messy snacks.

## Leave at home

• Phones, smartwatches, calculators, and notes. Confiscated devices can void your exam.
• Gates close at **7:30 a.m.** Late examinees are not admitted. Arrive by **6:30**.

## The night before

Do a **ten-item warm-up**, not a full mock. A full mock the night before only creates fatigue and anxiety. Sleep **seven to eight hours**; recall drops sharply below six.

## During the test

• Eat a real breakfast. The Professional exam runs **three hours and ten minutes** with no extended break.
• Answer everything, leave **nothing blank**, and check your answer sheet alignment every **25 items**.
